author: ROAPE
title: Before there is anything to punish: Burkina Faso’s new citizenship question
content:
On July 16, 2026, when addressing the

Forces vives

 in Yagha Province, Burkina Faso’s transitional president Captain Ibrahim Traoré referred to a statistic that seemed to take even him by surprise. “The number of young Burkinabè studying sharia law abroad is already at one thousand,” he said, and is still rising. Speaking in the context of Burkina Faso’s long-running jihadist insurgency, Traoré suggested that religious education abroad is risky because it can expose young Burkinabè to extremist interpretations of Islam beyond the state’s oversight. He then warned the students to return home, and that failure to do so could lead to them losing their Burkinabè citizenship.


The comment was notable for its religious overtones and some outlets, including members of my WhatsApp group chat where a picture of Traoré with the quote was being shared, seemed to celebrate it as a sign of proactive good governance. But I would say the most interesting thing about Traoré’s comments lies elsewhere. The proposed trigger is the decision to study sharia law abroad. In this sense, citizenship is made conditional before any charge of criminal behaviour, affiliation with a banned group, or participation in political violence. Thus, the threshold is now an educational choice. This deserves more attention because it departs from the way in which the deprivation of citizenship has generally been justified elsewhere.


In the past two decades, governments in countries such as France and the United Kingdom have broadened powers to revoke citizenship, in the name of national security. These measures have been subject to ongoing criticism from lawyers, activists, scholars, and civil liberties organisations concerned about due process and unequal citizenship. However, they have tended to be based on claims of certain conducts: the state provides evidence that some alleged act has been committed or shows a relationship with an organisation deemed to be a threat to security.


So, the present controversy revolves around whether those claims suffice to have a person’s citizenship revoked. But Traoré’s proposal is of a different order. The issue is not that these young Burkinabè have committed any offence, or that there is proven affiliation; the issue is their decision to take advantage of a particular form of education abroad. It looks like the concern precedes the specific matter to be investigated. And this raises a very unusual question: can citizenship itself be conditioned on what the state perceives as a person’s future life trajectory?


In the end, what this will augur for the legal code in Burkina Faso remains to be seen. But even as political rhetoric, the speech is a window into how security can migrate into areas that have traditionally escaped its reach.


Timing is also an important factor, because if the speech had been made in isolation, it might have been dismissed as an off-the-cuff intervention made before a local audience. But recent events point to a larger trend. In May 2026, Burkina Faso

suspended the country’s largest student union for three months

 after it publicly criticised the government. Government officials said the organisation was acting in a way that did not match its educational role. The suspension followed a familiar junta script in which political dissent by students was presented as a problem of public disorder. Barely a month later, another measure got far less international attention. Students from Burkina Faso seeking to pursue higher education abroad

will have to get government authorisation first

. So, going abroad to study is now a matter of prior state approval, not a private educational choice.


When taken together, these developments suggest a slow but steady increase in the government’s control over pathways to educational mobility, through the repositioning of study abroad and student unions within the same field of security governance. However, Traoré’s remarks about citizenship extend this one step further by linking the possibility of nationality itself to personal educational decisions.


There is also a regional dimension to take note of. A day after Traore’s address, the Council of Ministers in Mali

announced proposed amendments to its own citizenship law

, expanding the ability of the state to strip people of nationality under certain circumstances. Until now, there is no public evidence that the Burkinabè and Malian initiatives have been coordinated. It is much too early to …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Abdurahman Nur
title: After the Ballot: What Democracy Must Mean for Somalia
content:
Somali political life is intensely debated across towns, households, media platforms and diaspora communities. Yet this energy does not consistently produce the power to compel answers, reverse failed policies or remove officials whose conduct has become unacceptable. The distance between participation and political consequence remains one of Somalia’s central democratic problems.


Direct local elections in Puntland and Mogadishu have provided recent precedents, and

Somalia is again moving towards direct national elections.

 The framework for federal elections, however, has yet to be settled between the government and opposition. The debate should not stop at how votes will be cast. It must also ask what power citizens retain after they have cast them.


Somalia’s First Republic combined universal suffrage and competitive elections with legal opposition,

constitutionally protected civil freedoms and a government required to retain the National Assembly’s confidence

.


The 1969 election produced substantial turnover.

77 of the National Assembly’s 123 sitting members were not returned, including eight members of the outgoing cabinet

. The Somali Youth League (SYL), the governing party at the time, won 73 seats, while parties outside it secured 50. Political scientist Ahmed I. Samatar records that, when the new Assembly first met, all but one of the newly elected non-SYL deputies crossed to the governing party.


The formal result stood. Inside Parliament, most of the opposition strength it had created was gone. That is political attenuation: the balance created by voters remained on paper while losing much of its force inside Parliament. In this case, the attenuation occurred between the election and the new Parliament.


The same election also exposed pressure on the institution meant to keep the contest fair. The government asked police commander Mohamed Abshir Muse to place police personnel and vehicles at the disposal of the governing SYL in electorally important areas. Abshir had defended the force’s political neutrality. He refused and submitted his resignation. A temporary compromise placed him on leave until after the election. Tom J. Farer records that, during his absence, a northern commander known for integrity and political neutrality was recalled to Mogadishu, while more compliant officers were reportedly assigned to important electoral districts. Abshir’s resignation was then accepted.


A delegate casts his vote during the electoral process to choose members of the Lower House of the Somali federal Parliament in Baidoa, Somalia on November 25, 2016. UN Photo/ Sabir Olad


The police were responsible for protecting the election — the government asked them to help it win instead. The episode showed how vulnerable institutional neutrality became when it obstructed those already in power.


Somalia’s current political order was shaped by successive ruptures: colonial division, the discrediting of civilian government, military rule, state collapse and fragmented reconstruction. By 1969, civilian government had lost so much public confidence that the military takeover was widely welcomed. After the state collapsed, political reconstruction relied on a different settlement.


Somalia’s

4.5 formula

, a clan based power-sharing system, allocates equal shares of political representation to four major clan families and a collective half-share to minority groups. It helped restore representation, but also established guaranteed shares and gatekeeping roles for elders and political brokers that have proved difficult to dislodge. The arrangement continued to shape political choices as the surrounding context changed. That persistence is a form of political hysteresis. Research by the Somali Dialogue Platform and Somali Public Agenda describes both its contribution to inclusion and its concentration of political selection among a relatively small group of intermediaries.


Direct elections would return the choice of national representatives to citizens, but they would not automatically remove the political arrangements built around the present system. Candidate selection, party formation and coalition bargaining would still determine how much influence citizens retain after voting. Whether representatives remain visible to those who elected them, whether government answers Parliament and whether political decisions are actually carried out would remain separate questions.


The problem also appears after …

author: Akal Mohan
title: The Quiet Struggle of a Non-Practicing Christian
content:
“Between religion and my black skin there shall be a sky’s distance until the day I hear the call to atonement.”-Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor, The Dragonfly Sea


I feel like a fraud writing about religion. I feel so because I am an African who was Christian, yet I know very little about African Christianity. My (initial) faith was mostly informed by Western Christianity. It was embedded in the Seventh Day Adventist Church. I was born into, schooled in, and had lived by the Adventist teachings for most of my life. It is a denomination I am still indoctrinated by. If you know nothing about the Adventist Church, here is what you should know: It is a faith that is to date rooted in doctrines that have remained static over the years. Their command and church manual is universal and whereas context and culture should be considered in every religious practice, the Adventist Church regards them as inapt. Their global governing body is known as the General Conference and has its offices in Maryland, United States. This General Conference, you should know, has never had a black president since it was founded in 1863. To its staunch members, questioning the doctrines is perceived to be pillorying the church. The ultimate consequence of this is excommunication.


I give this background as a backdrop to why I am never confident writing about religion. Frankly, I have very little stake in what happens in the Church. I left Christianity half a decade ago and I have identified as agnostic ever since. I am agnostic, not atheist, because I understand that religiosity is a spiritual reality I cannot escape. “We are all religious beings,” Kenyan writer, philosopher and theologian Joe Kobuthi

says

. Joe proceeds to explain that the questions of life and meaning – existential questions – are all theological questions. I agree with Joe. My life, as I continue to experience it, is theology. My consciousness and temperament are grounded in biblical teachings. Much of the gospel is inductive to my life.


My quandary with religion and faith and belief continues to cause a disquiet in my spiritual life. The closest I can come to explaining this internal crisis is by using the words of Mahatma Gandhi in his work, “The Missionary and the Mission” where he states: “I am becoming humble enough to say that I cannot adequately represent the religion I practise by speech and pen. Language is a limitation of the truth which cannot only be represented by life.”  Gandhi’s disconcert might be limited to language and truth; my prejudice as an African extends further. Further because of the infusion of imperialism and colonization in the theology that has been passed down to me. This prejudice has overarching currents. It stays with an individual, a society, a culture and has led to a shift of indigenous moral pillars in African communities, as Dr Mwikamba has argued in his

paper

 “Changing Morals in Africa”. It is a tragedy that many Africans, me leading, cannot articulate what their true theological truth is. 


Anytime I see congregants gathered, praying in piety, I am reminded of how staunch I once was. I recall how I registered for outreach, attended fellowships, went out for mission work. These ministries gave me a tribe. It always felt like we were disciples of the same body, plighted by the same agony of bringing the lost back to Christ. We went out, our hearts devoted to The Great Commission: “Go ye and make disciples of all nations.” I have not lived in that desire for the last five years. It is a desire that I have shelved in my soul as I try to figure out what theology is practical in my reality. “Something repels the heart deeply in most organized forms of religion,” observes South African writer Bessie Head. This has been my struggle with organized religion: Its near cultic grip repels my heart. I am also occupied by the dilemmas of how to translate The Great Commission into my daily life. “We are too focused on heaven that our faith has no earthly relevance,” a pastor once said.   


***


The late Kenyan bishop and theologian Henry Okullu, in his essay, “Church and State”, opens by stating that, “One of the great issues in East Africa on which there is much confusion concerns the relationship which exists, or which should exist, between Church and State.”  Bishop Okullu, who championed pluralistic democracy and human rights, continues to write that every time the issue of the Church and State emerges, both politicians and Christians are …

author: Mada Masr
title: What’s behind the US sanctions on Banque Misr UAE?
content:
For Egyptian officials, the singling out of Banque Misr UAE in American sanctions was shocking, even if there are multiple rationales through which the move could be read.


The announcement of sanctions that came on Friday was the latest move in America’s new strategy to suffocate Iran. In mid August, United States President Donald Trump let it be known that he was fed up. After months of negotiations with Iran over an end to a war, a war that the US and Israel started, had failed to materialize, it was time to change tactics. 


This time, it wouldn’t be a new naval blockade on an existing naval blockade. It wouldn’t be more military action.

This time, Trump

wrote

 on his social media account, the pain would come in the form of the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.”


Essentially, the plan, dubbed “Economic D-Day,” a reference to the US invasion of Nazi-held France during World War II, would see Washington DC impose secondary sanctions on any country that “allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran.”


Swooping in to take up the messaging of the plan, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began to beat the war drum of economic sanctions. 


“If you insist on doing business with [Iran], then the US Treasury and U.S. government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent

said

 on August 20.

 “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”


The media was awash in speculation. Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are among Iran’s largest trade partners. Would the US really consider sanctioning such key allies?


And then the decisive day came. On Friday, the US treasury

announced

 its first salvo. 


First to be sanctioned was Reza Mohammad Taeedi, the manager of the Iranian commercial bank Bank Melli’s Dubai branch. 


It made sense: an Iranian bank operating in Dubai surely must be part of a shadow banking operation. 


Next was Kameng Trading Limited, a Hong Kong-based exchange company that has allegedly helped launder funds for a sanctioned Iranian exchange house. 


Again, the proximity to China, which is known to have relations with Iran, made the move legible. 


But the last entity included in the sanctions notice was a surprise. The United Arab Emirates branches of Banque Misr, the Egyptian state-owned bank and the second largest in Egypt, holding assets worth US$83 billion, could see its banking access to US financial institutions revoked, the US treasury announced.


Describing the five branches of what is Egypt’s second largest bank, the US treasury note called the bank “a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to US dollars. Treasury estimates that between January 2024 and June 2026, Banque Misr UAE processed approximately $1.8 billion for 103 companies that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks.”


“Banque Misr UAE’s customers include apparent front companies used by Iran’s Ministry of Defense and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to evade US sanctions, as well as to launder money on behalf of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei,” the statement read. 


The US treasury has given Banque Misr 30 days before the sanctions take effect. In the meantime, it is accepting comments from the public, industry experts and financial institutions about the proposed sanction. 


While the reasons are still unknown, the decision did not materialize out of thin air.


Since around 2023, Egypt has faced a new difficult reality. 


A $23 billion deal with Saudi Arabia inked in 2016 had expired, and while the initial deal had been greased with the handover of Tiran and Sanafir islands, Egypt and Saudi relations had taken a turn for much rockier shores. While the deal extended beyond its initial five-year timeframe, by 2023, Saudi Arabia was no longer willing to provide discounted fuel for Egypt at a time when repeated economic crises were wrecking the country and mounting debt repayments loomed, according to an Egyptian state official who spoke to Mada Masr in early 2025.


To address the shortfall, Egypt had to turn to unconventional solutions at a price that could be affordable. And for Egypt, as for many countries in the region, this meant one thing: Iran.

author: ROAPE
title: The murder of Professor Jason Arday
content:
On Sunday 16 August I joined the vigil for Professor Arday in London’s Trafalgar Square in the summer’s heat, packed tight with thousands of protestors marking their respect, holding bunches of flowers aloft, and placards reading, ‘Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday.’ Heads bowed, hundreds around me in tears – the words of his students unbearable, our anger craving a response. 


Professor Arday is dead. Murdered. Yet again another Black person has been killed – pilloried in a public execution orchestrated by a profoundly racist press, and organised fascists.


The vigil spoke to the structural racism that shaped Professor Arday’s life and death. I was struck by British MP Diane Abbott’s comments on the Black experience in the UK and the racism encountered daily. This daily experience is engrained in British institutions, the press and political life.


His family commented about the outpouring of grief and fury, describing their emotions: ‘The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.’


Bittersweet indeed – the kindness, support and grief were essential but too late. 


Professor Jason Arday – the Black professor of sociology at Cambridge University – was hounded to his death by a racist campaign to unseat him from his position. In the 22 days leading to his suicide, there were 249 articles in major newspapers in the UK, continual coverage on TV, radio and blogs. This had followed a repeated effort to undermine Arday since he became a professor at the university in 2023.


The noise from this pogrom – accusing him of plagiarism, lies, bombast, academic fakery – was overwhelming. Many people who should have known better joined the chorus. The UK’s mainstream liberal paper, 

The Guardian,

 

launched an investigation into Arday’s scholarship

. I encountered family members who joined in the chorus – denouncing Arday, ridiculing his claims, and his work.


On 5 August, Arday resigned from his post; the following week, on 14 August, he committed suicide. A man described by his students as ‘gentle’, ‘caring’, ‘compassionate’ and ‘inspiring’ was systematically broken – destroyed in a campaign which led directly to his suicide. 


Arday was murdered. 


This was the objective – Arday’s suicide was the logical outcome. Leading the recent crusade was the racist scholar, Nathan Cofnas, who published on his Substack the blog, ‘

DEI Fraud and Cover-Up at Cambridge

’, on 21 July 2026.  A vile man who targeted and conducted his own investigation into Arday’s work  – charging him with plagiarism, which confirmed Cofnas’ thesis that Black people are inferior, unworthy of senior academic positions. 


Cofnas is a symptom of our times. A marginal, bigoted voice that once would have remained largely undetected in the swamp is now amplified by a mainstream, racist agenda. In the global North, these voices have reached fever pitch – finding traction in a political climate that has seen right-wing governments elected, and racist policies normalised in daily political speech. 


To say these developments are worrying is a grotesque understatement – these are clarion signs of our current and deepening crisis, and the irredeemable racism of our political and economic system. This cannot be absorbed and understood simply as a British thing. We see the same tightening of the screw in the personal attacks on International Criminal Court judges and the normalisation of genocide.


There are three observations that I want to make in this piece. Firstly, I want to look at two political parallels –  one that prompted the global mass movement, Black Lives Matter, a few years ago, and the second when antisemitism was denounced by the French author Émile Zola at the end of the 19

th

 century. Finally, I want to say a few things about plagiarism and academia. 


On 25 May 2020 in Minneapolis, George Floyd was stopped by the police, then wrestled to the ground by police officer Derek Chauvin – clips of his slow death over nine minutes were beamed across the planet. Chauvin was later convicted of murder. George Floyd was choked to death by Chauvin, who pinned Floyd to the ground, as he died – filmed by the incredibly brave 17-year-old Darnella Frazie – he was heard saying,‘Mama, mama, mama’, ‘Momma, I love you,’ and ‘Momma! I’m through.’


George Floyd was …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies: A Community of Practice to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence
content:
Over the past year, Liberation Alliance Africa has sustained the

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Indigenous Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

. This Community of Practice is a collective of African feminist scholars, practitioners, organisers, artists, and movement builders committed to the dreaming and making of a world free from sexual violence through knowledge bridges.


Sexual violence continues to impact communities across the African continent, and class, ethnicity and religion play a critical role in making civilians in conflict-affected countries particularly more vulnerable. It disproportionately affects women and girls, and ethnic, gender and racialized minorities. Sexual violence is compounded by conflict, displacement, poverty, and gender inequality. It remains significantly under-reported due to stigma and under-prosecuted? Due to weak and corrupt justice systems. Sexual violence includes rape and sexual assault, sexual coercion and exploitation, including trafficking for sexual exploitation and conflict-related sexual violence such as using rape as a weapon of war. It affects people of any gender and age. 


Our starting premise is simple: sexual violence on the continent cannot be understood, let alone addressed, through frameworks that treat colonialism as history rather than a structural force that continues to shape theory, practice, and response to sexual violence. 


Coloniality was

coined

by Peruvian philosopher and sociologist Aníbal Quijano, and it describes the long-lasting pattern of power produced by colonial rule and shape

s

 how we approach epistemological frameworks through which violence is understood.

Epistemology deals with questions concerning the nature, scope, and sources of knowledge.

 A meaningful analysis of sexual violence must begin by seeking to decolonise knowledge and epistemic structures. This analysis requires us to interrogate the assumptions that underpin dominant theories, question whose expertise is legitimised, and create space for African feminist epistemologies to shape how violence is understood, prevented, and responded to. 


We felt an urgent need to organise as scholars and practitioners to generate new frameworks grounded in our histories, political realities, and lived experiences. Our analyses are rooted in our confrontation of the neo-colonial state, the global imperialist, extractive and patriarchal systems that shape our everyday existence. We arrive as feminists in service of a liberatory project, convinced that knowledge-making is itself a site of feminist struggle. 


As the CoP came together through both intentional convening and organic growth, we began organising our work around three enquiries that we believe are critical to envisioning a decolonial feminist approach to preventing and responding to sexual violence in Africa. 


The first enquiry,

Whose Knowledge? An Audit of the Current Knowledge Systems within Sexual Violence Prevention and Response in Africa

 examines the dominant literature, asks whose voices have shaped the field, whose knowledge has been marginalised, and what becomes possible when African feminist scholarship is placed at the centre of analysis. 


The second enquiry,

 The Coloniality of Sexual Violence: Gender, Power, Sovereignty, and the Neo-Colonial State,

 advances interventions on sexual violence that explicitly interrogate the role and impact of hetero-patriarchal colonial racial-capitalism, alongside the complicity of neo-colonial states, in producing and sustaining conditions of gendered violence. 


The third enquiry,

Truth-telling and Epistemic Sovereignty in the Prevention and Response Continuum

, centres on indigenous and endogenous knowledge systems as essential practice-based frameworks for reimagining prevention, response, healing, accountability, and collective safety.


The Imperative of Recentering African Epistemologies


At Liberation Alliance Africa, we believe African women and gender-expansive people’s knowledge-making and world-building are crucial to de-westernising normative assumptions and dominant approaches. African women and gender-expansive scholars must nurture new ways of knowing and being- knowledge that doesn’t just challenge dominant views, but creates a rich foundation for how we understand reality and tackle life’s critical questions.


For a long time, African women and gender minorities were treated as …

author: Randi Beers
title: There’s no place like home
content:
Before John Amagoalik returned to Nunavut this summer, he said the

first things on his mind

 would be the taste of Arctic clams and the kiss he would place on his wife’s cheek.


His arrival at Iqaluit’s airport on June 12 was a significant moment. Nunavut is a territory thanks in part to Amagoalik.


The 78-year-old had been living at Embassy West, a long-term care centre located in Ottawa, for 16 months when his

 loved ones came together earlier this year to help him spend the final days of his life in Nunavut.


They raised money for his move, procured at-home medical support and negotiated subsidized housing. But they warned they would need help from the Department of Health to fund his care in the long term.


Now, the department is saying it can only fund a fraction of the support he needs, meaning that, after

 all that work to bring him home, the man revered by many as the Father of Nunavut

might have to return

 to Ottawa.


The territorial government recognizes the importance of providing elder care closer to home. It’s written all over its

 elders strategy, released in 2024.


It’s unclear how much the government was paying Embassy West to look after Amagoalik, but his friends and family used publicly available numbers to estimate it could have been in the area of $32,000 per month.

The cost to provide his housing and care in Iqaluit is about half that, they say.


It doesn’t matter if it’s cheaper to stay in Iqaluit, say the top brass at the Department of Health.


“Privately contracted care services and independent housing arrangements remain separate from department-funded Home Care Services. Consequently, they cannot be provided or funded through the department’s Home Care Program,”

wrote Heather Hair, assistant deputy minister of health, to Amagoalik and his representatives on Aug. 14.


“The department is not responsible for housing and is unable to transfer funds allocated to existing elder facility contracts to pay for private housing for individuals.”


This issue isn’t just about Amagoalik, and I would never suggest he is owed preferential treatment because of his career.


It is about hamstrung bureaucrats, unable to meet an individual on his own terms because policies prevent ingenuity.


How many elders across the territory are in the same situation as Amagoalik, for whom there is a feasible and economic way to provide in-territory care if somebody approved a tailor-made plan? If there is even one, that’s too many.


Does the Department of Health employ staff to work with elders and their families, to explore options to provide support in the territory? Are they allowed to think outside policies if it’s financially feasible and possibly better for an elder? If not, why not?


Everybody agrees it’s better for elders to age at home. In Amagoalik’s case at least, it appears it could be cheaper, too.


Amagoalik grew up governed by federal policies. He saw they didn’t work for Nunavut, so he upended them.


His situation today is a challenge to the government he helped create. If a policy isn’t working, it can be changed.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Community mourns Joan Phillip, Amshen, who fought for justice and ‘loved very hard’
content:
Joan Phillip, Amshen, stands next to the Grandview Park Cenotaph in 2024. She passed away on Aug. 28, 2026, at the age of 74.

Photo by Kayla MacInnis


Fearless. Fierce. Wise. Courageous. Cherished.


Those were just a few of the words that colleagues and loved ones used to describe the late Joan Phillip, Amshen, at her funeral service in snpink’tn (Penticton, B.C.) on Wednesday. 


Before Amshen was laid to rest in the community cemetery in syilx Okanagan homelands, leaders, dignitaries, and people from near and far packed the Outma Sqilx’W Cultural School’s gym — with hundreds more watching a livestream online — to remember the beloved leader.


“It was one of the dreams and hopes of our people for years to have our own school in our community to teach our children. Joan helped get this here,” said caxasket Joseph Pierre of the Penticton Indian Band (PIB), who moderated the funeral service.


Amshen,

an Indigenous leader and lifelong activist from the Tsleil-Waututh Nation

, died last Friday on Aug. 28, at the age of 74. Her grandfather was the late Chief Dan George.


At the time of her death, she was serving as a member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) of British Columbia. She represented the Vancouver-Strathcona riding — previously Vancouver-Mount Pleasant — through the NDP, a position she held since 2023.


‘Do not be afraid to stand like Joan stood’


Amshen spent more than 20 years as the lands administrator for PIB, retiring from that role in 2019. She was a member of the Penticton Band Council and married to Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, the president of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, who was chief of PIB for 14 years. The couple split their time between “Vancouver” and snpink’tn.


“I thank the Creator, I thank kʷuləncutn, for putting Joan on my path — for herself and my path,” the Grand Chief said at Amshen’s funeral, whom he had grown to know as “Bunny” during their marriage.


“We were able to have such a wonderful life together.  I feel no regrets. My heart is in a good place. I feel gratitude. I feel amazing, powerful gratitude, that I had the opportunity to be together with Joan. To share her life, to share her love, to share her principles and integrity.”


A staunch advocate for Indigenous title and rights; the wellbeing of the land and for future generations, Amshen’s relatives recalled a woman “who had no fear” and “stood up” against colonial injustices.


“Joan was all about children, young people, our Elders. People in the Downtown Eastside absolutely loved Joan, because they knew she was there for them,” said the Grand Chief.


People shared stories of her involvement with the Red Power Movement and the Native Alliance for Red Power when she was just 16 years old, as well as her moments of solidarity with the Oka Crisis, the Gustafsen Lake standoff, and Standing Rock.


In one of her final acts in the fight for the rights of Indigenous Peoples, Amshen stood up against B.C. Premier David Eby and her own political party earlier this year, when attempts were made to amend the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).


“I was so proud of her,” Phillip said of his late wife and her opposition to amend DRIPA.


“We’re not oil people in this room. We’re not pipeline people. We’re not corporate people. We’re Indians. That was the beauty of Joan — she knew that. She knew which team she was on, and why she was on that team.”


While they mourned her loss, the Grand Chief and others in Amshen’s close circle encouraged people in the room to honour her legacy by continuing on with the work that she had committed her life to.


“When we move forward in the work that’s ahead of us, do not be afraid to stand like Joan stood,” said the Grand Chief.


“Don’t be afraid to stand up. Joan’s principle was: we have to stand up, no matter what. So I ask you to do that.”


Stewart and Joan Phillip stand with their fists in the air against Kinder Morgan on Burnaby Mountain.

‘That legacy needs to carry on’


Eby was in attendance for Amshen’s funeral, and was the first guest invited to speak at her service. While acknowledging that it was a difficult day for everyone in the room, he described his colleague as “a remarkable person with such incredible history in our province.”


“Joan was absolutely fearless. She’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. And she was an incredible friend and colleague,” said Eby.

author: Gary Chartier
title: Pro-Pasar, Anti-“Kapitalisme”
content:
Gary Chartier

. Teks aslinya berjudul ‘

Embracing Markets, Opposing “Capitalism

”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa


Menjadi seorang libertarian berarti menolak penggunaan kekerasan untuk membatasi pertukaran yang berlangsung secara damai dan sukarela. Namun, hal itu tidak berarti bahwa libertarianisme harus dipahami sebagai dukungan terhadap kapitalisme.


Apakah klaim ini masuk akal atau tidak, tentu bergantung pada apa yang Anda maksud dengan “kapitalisme”. Bagi sebagian orang, mungkin istilah tersebut sekadar merujuk pada pertukaran bebas. Jika memang itu yang Anda maksud ketika berbicara tentang “kapitalisme”, Anda benar bahwa tidak ada pertentangan nyata antara apa yang Anda maksud dan libertarianisme yang masuk akal.


Namun, ketika menggunakan istilah tersebut, orang sering kali memiliki pengertian lain dalam pikirannya. Misalnya, media cetak dan elektronik arus utama secara rutin menggunakan “kapitalisme” untuk merujuk pada “sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini”. Cukup umum pula mendengar “kapitalisme” digunakan sebagai sinonim dari “dominasi kapitalis atas tempat kerja dan masyarakat – yakni dominasi oleh para pemilik aset modal dalam jumlah besar”. Prinsip-prinsip libertarian, sebagaimana saya memahaminya, tidak mengharuskan dukungan terhadap kapitalisme dalam kedua pengertian tersebut.


Dalam tingkat yang sangat signifikan

, sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini justru merupakan sistem yang di dalamnya pertukaran damai dan sukarela tidak sepenuhnya hadir. Jaringan hak istimewa yang dibentuk oleh hukum dan regulasi saling terkait memberikan keuntungan kepada orang-orang kaya dan mereka yang memiliki koneksi politik, dengan mengorbankan orang lain (misalnya paten dan hak cipta, tarif, pembatasan perbankan, aturan perizinan profesi, pembatasan penggunaan lahan, dan sebagainya). Kompleks industri-militer mengalirkan uang dalam jumlah yang sulit dipercaya – dengan todongan senjata – dari kantong masyarakat biasa ke rekening para kontraktor pemerintah dan kroni-kroninya. Berbagai bentuk subsidi memberi makan jaringan hak istimewa bagi perusahaan maupun organisasi nirlaba. Negara juga melindungi kepemilikan atas tanah yang diperoleh dengan todongan senjata atau dikuasai melalui keputusan sepihak sebelum kemudian dibagikan kepada individu dan kelompok yang disukai. Memang, setidaknya perekonomian Amerika Serikat, Kanada, Eropa Barat, Jepang, dan Australia bukanlah perekonomian yang direncanakan secara terpusat. Negara juga tidak secara formal mengklaim kepemilikan atas (sebagian besar) alat-alat produksi. Namun, keterlibatan negara di berbagai tingkat dalam menjamin dan memperkuat hak-hak istimewa ekonomi membuat sistem ekonomi yang kita miliki saat ini sulit disebut sebagai sistem yang bebas. Jadi, jika “kapitalisme” digunakan untuk menyebut sistem yang kita miliki sekarang, siapa pun yang mendukung kebebasan memiliki alasan kuat untuk bersikap skeptis terhadap kapitalisme.


Hak-hak istimewa yang menjadi ciri tatanan ekonomi yang ada saat ini, apa pun nama yang kita gunakan untuk menyebutnya, secara tidak proporsional menguntungkan mereka yang memiliki pengaruh politik paling besar dan kekayaan paling besar. Jaringan hak istimewa yang dipertahankan oleh negara juga, dalam berbagai cara, cenderung memperkuat posisi istimewa para kapitalis di tempat kerja. Dalam konteks tempat kerja, hak istimewa yang dijamin negara mengurangi kemungkinan orang untuk bekerja secara mandiri (dengan meningkatkan kebutuhan modal dan berbagai biaya masuk lainnya, sekaligus mengurangi sumber daya yang mungkin dapat digunakan seseorang untuk memulai dan mempertahankan usahanya sendiri). Negara juga memberlakukan pembatasan terhadap aktivitas serikat pekerja yang mengurangi kemampuan pekerja untuk melakukan tawar-menawar secara efektif dengan pemberi kerja. Dengan mengurangi alternatif selain pekerjaan berupah dan mempersempit peluang pekerja untuk melakukan perundingan kolektif, negara secara substansial meningkatkan daya tawar pemberi kerja. Singkatnya, dominasi “kapitalis” atas tempat kerja dan masyarakat tidak dapat dipahami dalam bentuknya yang sekarang tanpa memperhatikan campur tangan dan penyimpangan yang dilakukan negara. Sekali lagi, jika inilah yang disebut “kapitalisme”, para pendukung kebebasan tidak memiliki alasan untuk menerimanya.


Tentu saja, masuk akal jika seseorang berpendapat bahwa meskipun “kapitalisme” sering digunakan untuk merujuk pada fenomena sosial yang patut dipersoalkan …

author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: The US Brought the G20 to NC to Highlight the Region’s Hurricane Recovery. Locals Say the Government Wasn’t Who Made it Possible.
content:
Asheville, NC — Last weekend, the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors met in Asheville at the behest of the U.S. federal government. Billed as an opportunity to showcase the region’s recovery after Hurricane Helene laid waste to western North Carolina in 2024, locals took issue with their suffering and hard work being co-opted by representatives of the world’s richest countries.


After the Department of Treasury

announced

 in February that the meeting would take place in the Appalachian town, locals began organizing.


In the weeks before the meeting, organizers hosted a series of events and worked to spread the word about the finance ministers who had set their sites on Asheville’s Omni Grove Park Inn as their venue.


By the time delegates arrived on Saturday, August 29, a slew of organizations and unaffiliated locals had prepared a weekend of events to highlight that the often-overlooked meeting was taking place and emphasize that they, not the government or economists, were the ones who did the work of rebuilding the area after the storm.


Starting on Friday, groups of protesters took space on bridges spanning the interstate that runs by downtown Asheville. Holding banners, locals decried the presence of the finance ministers who arrived in their town that day. On at least three bridges, organizers draped banners with messages including “Asheville rejects technofascism” and “workers over billionaires.”


“We think they’re more focused on corporate interests and the interests of the wealthy over the interests of everyday people and working people,” Rachel Cohen, local policy lead of Sunrise Movement Western North Carolina, told Unicorn Riot.


Cohen’s suspicion is supported by the group’s history. The G20, or

Group of 20

, is a coalition of the world’s 20 largest economies made up of 19 member countries, the European Union and the African Union. The finance track, which meets four times a year leading up to the annual global summit, sets policy and determines the focus of the broader group.


Among the forum’s stated goals is to ensure economic stability and cooperation, but historically the body has worked to prop up capitalism in moments of crisis.


The G20 was formed in 1999 following the

Asian market collapse

 brought on by

financial manipulation

 from foreign investors who saw vulnerabilities in booming southeast Asian economies. After Thailand’s baht collapsed, the International Monetary Fund loaned Thailand and other countries caught in the turmoil billions of dollars to be repaid with interest, prompting a steep rise in unemployment, poverty and a decrease in social welfare spending.


In 2008, after the U.S. housing bubble burst and sent the economy into a tailspin, the G20 held its first global summit to respond to the crisis facing U.S. markets and capitalism’s legitimacy. Called by President George W. Bush to address a problem bigger than any one government could resolve,

the G20 assembled

 to develop solutions to the collapsing economy and ensure continued, perpetual growth.


Every year since, a member country has hosted the annual G20 summit as well as a series of satellite meetings that direct the group’s policies and mission. This year, the U.S. is hosting the G20, and last weekend’s gathering represented one of the finance track’s series of meetings leading up to the global summit to be hosted this December in Miami.


As vehicles honked in support during last Friday’s banner display, residents told Unicorn Riot that the G20 meeting in their town specifically to highlight the recovery post-Helene glossed over the reality of the situation.


Locals, like those waving banners from the bridges that afternoon, and nearby supporters responded to the crisis and are continuing the ongoing work of rebuilding the area, not the G20 or the entities they represent, Cohen said to UR.


The following morning, approximately 150 protesters spread out along Merrimon Avenue just north of downtown Asheville to oppose the meeting and continue to spread their message. There, along the busy thoroughfare, protesters waved signs and recalled who was present in the aftermath of the hurricane nearly two years earlier.


Lola Lafey, a local who lived through the storm, told Unicorn Riot that the first responders she saw were locals and neighbors, and that the federal government didn’t play as big a role as they needed to in the days after Helene.

author: FMF Staff
title: Statement of the Feminist Majority Foundation on the Death of Gloria Steinem
content:
Gloria Steinem, a lifelong champion of women’s equality and co-founder of Ms. magazine, died Sept. 2, 2026, at age 92. For more than half a century, Steinem helped bring feminist ideas, voices and movements into the mainstream through journalism, organizing and activism—and helped build Ms. into what it remains today: not simply a magazine, but a movement.

“When Steinem and the other owners of Ms. entrusted the magazine to the Feminist Majority Foundation, we understood that we were being entrusted with far more than a publication,” said Katherine Spillar, executive director of Feminist Majority Foundation and executive editor of Ms. “We were being asked to preserve an independent feminist institution, and to keep it alive, questioning and relevant for generations that would face battles we could not yet foresee. That responsibility is more urgent today than at any time in recent memory.”

Today, Ms. magazine is thriving. In print and online it reaches tens of thousands of readers every day and over 4.5 million readers a year. It has not only maintained consistent print circulation throughout the pandemic and the overall decline of print media, but has also seen its web presence skyrocket through its website, social media, and the podcasts it publishes through Ms. Studio. Ms. can also be found in thousands of libraries and classrooms, where new generations encounter feminist journalism, history and ideas that might otherwise never reach them.

“Gloria understood the importance of independent feminist media from the beginning,” said Eleanor Smeal, publisher of Ms. and president of the Feminist Majority Foundation. “Ms. remains an independent, nonprofit, feminist newsroom that is not beholden to commercial advertisers. That independence allows Ms. to keep breaking new ground, just as Gloria intended. From reproductive freedom and violence against women to pay equity, political representation and the global struggle for human rights, Ms. continues to cover the issues affecting women long before much of the mainstream media recognizes their importance.”

Ms. Magazine was co-founded in 1972 by Gloria Steinem. Gloria asked the Feminist Majority Foundation to take over Ms. magazine, and the Feminist Majority Foundation has been the publisher of Ms. magazine since 2001.

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: US communities are organizing to end complicity with genocide in their backyards
content:
This article

US communities are organizing to end complicity with genocide in their backyards

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Dwight Hua’s roommate knocked on his door at 5:30 a.m. on May 22, saying there was a notice for

nearly 50,000 people in their city of Garden Grove

, California, to evacuate due to the danger of a deadly chemical explosion at a nearby GKN Aerospace plant. Hua quickly left for a shelter in a neighboring city. But he had a lot of questions. 


As the evacuation stretched over five days, advocacy groups VietRISE — where Hua is a youth programs coordinator — the Harbor Institute for Immigrant and Economic Justice, the Palestinian Youth Movement, and Orange County Justice for Palestine formed a coalition to demand “transparency about why a facility tied to global hazardous weapons manufacturing is operating in the middle of working-class immigrant neighborhoods.” Research led by the local chapter of the Palestinian Youth Movement, or PYM, found that the company manufactured parts for military vehicles, including F-35 fighter jets, which are used in Israel’s

ongoing genocide

 of Palestinians.


“No one really knew that this was what we were living close to,” Hua said. “A company that makes money off of violence abroad is not the character of Garden Grove and its residents.”


Many residents who, like Hua, live just blocks away from the facility felt enraged when they found out. The coalition joined the

People’s Embargo for Palestine

, an international movement to establish an arms embargo on Israel, and began organizing actions to push the city to shut down GKN Aerospace and place a moratorium on military manufacturing in Garden Grove. They have been canvassing, showing up to city council meetings and circulating a

petition that has drawn more than 11,000

 signatures. Addressed to the mayor and city council, the petition demands “an immediate end to the use of our tax dollars, public land and public infrastructure to manufacture, store or transport the weapons that make this genocide possible.” 


While the Garden Grove City Council has canceled meetings and omitted GKN Aerospace from meeting agendas in the months since the evacuation, Hua said, the coalition has kept on growing in size and influence. Members continue to show up to city council meetings, canvass and meet with city officials, some of whom have shown support for the embargo.


The campaign for a weapons embargo is part of a larger international movement to stop global manufacturing and shipment of weapons to Israel. From Türkiye to Italy to the U.S., localized campaigns targeted at Israeli weapons suppliers have emerged, led by community groups and unions, and often supported by PYM chapters. Their goal is to end local complicity in the genocide — and ensure worker and community safety — through bans on weapons shipments through local airports and seaports, as well as shutdowns and moratoriums on weapons manufacturing facilities in residential areas.


Putting communities at risk for Israel


A coalition of community groups is leading an embargo campaign in New York City’s John F. Kennedy Airport, where dangerous

explosives

 and F-35 bomber components bound for Israel have passed through the same runways as passenger flights. The campaign is calling on the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey to end arms shipments through public infrastructure. Most of the coalition’s efforts have been geared toward organizing and educating workers, especially unionized workers in warehouses and on planes.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Abdullah Shehadeh, communications co-chair of Break the Chain, the coalition leading the campaign, said that workers were unaware they were handling explosives bound for Israel because they were mislabeled. 


“Workers feel very scared about what they’re doing in their day to day, not knowing that complicity like this is even possible for them,” Shehadeh said. “They didn’t sign up to be part of a supply chain of genocide.”


In outreach to workers, volunteers with the coalition also point out the dangers of handling explosives, noting that a

munitions plant in Tennessee

 which manufactured the same explosives experienced a blast last year that destroyed an entire building and killed 16 people.

author: Valerie Anne
title: Everything You Need To Know About the Lesbians of ‘Silo’
content:
For the first two and a half seasons of the post-apocalyptic Apple TV epic Silo, we only had two lesbian characters, buried deep in the ground: a badass mechanic, Martha, played by Harriet Walter who rarely left her apartment, and her ex-wife Carla, head of Supply, played by Clare Perkins. Their relationship was not a major plotline, but I was happy for the representation anyway. Elder lesbians! The best at their respective jobs! Love to see it.

This season, we got introduced to some more lesbians, this time in the aboveground storyline. Congressman Daniel Keene finds out his younger sister Charlotte (Jessica Brown Findlay, who played queer on Harlots) had been in an accident while she was working as a Navy pilot. After she recovered, she joined her brother and the reporter Helen Drew (Jessica Henwick) to learn more about what brought her plane down, and there she met the Senator’s daughter Anna (Morven Christie). The two hit it off and were flirting on a private plane and I kind of thought that was the most we were going to get, but then the aboveground timeline had a little time jump and the next thing we know, Charlotte and Anna are married! They have a cute double-date night with Daniel and Helen and gosh you’d almost forget this was an apocalypse show.

However, at the end of the episode, Charlotte is nowhere to be found. Daniel tries to text her and gets a response that makes him suspicious she doesn’t have access to her own phone. I texted my friend, LESBIAN IN PERIL. Though based on how the episode ended…a lot more people than just Charlotte are in peril.

Now, for the majority of this season, I held onto a bonkers theory: I thought the aboveground and belowground timelines were running concurrently. I was so convinced the silos were a social experiment being done before any nukes had ever gone off. My theory was kiboshed by the end of the episode, HOWEVER, I still don’t think 300 years have passed between the aboveground timeline and what Juliette Nichols is up to. I think it’s possible it has only been 50 years, or fewer, and the Vitamin D+ they use to erase everyone’s memories, combined with the Pact and the “AI” voice, led them to believe it’s been a lot longer, telling them fictional stories about past rebellions and other resets. I think that’s why artifacts and relics were outlawed, lest they trigger memories. Otherwise, what would it matter if they had things from the old world? So now, my newest unhinged theory is: what if Charlotte IS Martha. This week, they talked about how the Vitamin D+ shakes memories up so bad some parents forgot to feed their own children. So it’s not unreasonable to think a person or two forgot their own name. And Navy pilot to mechanic isn’t an insane pipeline…JUST SAYING.

Anyway, I’ve been having a lot of fun trying to untangle the mysteries of this world, going full red string murderboard about it, and I am STRESSED but excited to see what Silo‘s season finale brings this week. Fingers crossed all lesbians will be found and accounted for, safe and sound and underground.

title: US Government Designates Host of NoBlogs.org a "Global Terrorist"
content:
On August 26, 2026, the United States government

classified

 the Italian collective Autistici/Inventati as a “Specially Designated Global Terrorist,” citing the collective’s “far-left” politics to justify the designation. They announced similar designations of the British group Palestine Action and the transnational Palestinian movement Masar Badil in the same statement.


Founded in 2001, Autistici/Inventati is a volunteer-run provider of privacy-oriented email, websites, mailing lists, blogs, and communications tools for users who prefer not to rely on corporate platforms. According to the US State Department, Autistici/Inventati hosts “roughly 16,000 mailboxes, 1,500 websites, 5,500 mailing lists, and 10,000 ‘blogs’ on its custom-built platform.”


Autistici/Inventati explain their values and goals in their

manifesto

:


We believe that communication must be free—and for free—and, therefore, universally accessible.


We try to accomplish all this by offering internet services (web sites, e-mail, mailing lists, chats, blogs, newsletters, and more) using our best skills and knowledge to defend both individuals or groups sharing our same aims or ideals. […]


We believe that media and communication should not be the exclusive domain of information professionals. We believe in the value of self-management: this is why we have no sponsors or funding of any kind, apart from voluntary donations from those who believe that our project is important and must survive. None of us earns a cent from this project (in fact, quite the opposite).


Many

book fairs

, radio programs, and other cultural projects rely on the Autistici/Inventati platform

noblogs.org

 for website hosting. According to one

anti-fascist research group

, “Some of the most well-known NoBlogs sites belong to researchers who solely report on far-right hate and radicalization, never doing anything aside from showing you what exists.” Such researchers helped to identify the fascists who participanted in the “Unite the Right” rally in 2017, during which one Neo-Nazi

murdered

 Heather Heyer in an

actual

 act of terrorism.


The US State Department is rationalizing this designation by alleging that Autistici/Inventati “provides encrypted tools and services to numerous violent far-left extremist groups,” including Portland-based Rose City Antifa. Their claim about Rose City Antifa seems to be

false

, however,

conflating

 Rose City Antifa with another project called Rose City Counterinfo.


On the basis of this error, the State Department rushed to

proclaim

 an alleged “Portland Antifa connection to Hamas” and “Iran’s IRGC” [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps], with the sole justification being the allegation that an unnamed “extremist media group”—which they do not allege had any relationship to Rose City Antifa—had republished statements from Hamas and the IRGC on a website hosted by noblogs.org. This is representative of the dishonesty and erroneousness of the State Department press release as a whole.


When a military force carries out an attack on a village, the first thing they do is attempt to cut the communication lines that connect it to the outside world. We have to understand the attack on Autistici/Inventati the same way. Now that tech corporations from

Meta

 to the

platform formerly known as Twitter

 have showed that they are willing to ban whoever the US government instructs them to, the US government is going after groups that provide web services on a non-commercial basis.


Because there is no “domestic terrorist organization” designation in the United States, the Trump administration began its

criminalization

 of anti-fascists by

designating

 European anti-fascist groups as “terrorists.” They are targeting an Italian tech project for the same reason: they aim to put the pieces in place to criminalize domestic protesters by associating them with designated “Global Terrorist” groups.


According to the United States

Department of the Treasury

, starting on September 25, 2026, any transactions with Autistici/Inventati will be “prohibited
by the Global Terrorism Sanctions Regulations.”

short statement

 about the designation:

author: Andrés
title: El Estado «fabrica la irregularidad» para justificar la cacería de migrantes
content:
Foto extraida de Tiempo Argentino. Sin autor/a.


Más de 2.000 efectivos policiales movilizados contra trabajadores que, en un 93,6%, no tenían ninguna falta migratoria. El informe desarma el relato oficial sobre la «amenaza extranjera» y expone el plan sistemático para frenar trámites, exigir requisitos fantasma y fomentar la xenofobia en medio de la crisis económica nacional.

Por Mario Canaviri para ANRed.


La criminalización de la pobreza y la estigmatización del migrante volvieron a ser política de Estado. Detrás del gran despliegue de policías federales y trabajadores de Migraciones, los datos oficiales desarman el relato gubernamental de la «amenaza» extranjera. Según un reciente informe del Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), basado en pedidos de acceso a la información pública, las fuerzas de seguridad federales montaron operativos que no logran justificación y solo hostigan a comunidades migrantes, ya estigmatizadas.


Durante el primer semestre de 2026, el Estado movilizó a más de 2.000 efectivos policiales —1.788 de ellos de la Policía Federal— para intervenir en 590 operativos callejeros. ¿El resultado de semejante despliegue?

El 93,6%

de las personas controladas (6.802 sobre un total de 7.261) eran extranjeros con

su condición migratoria completamente regular

.

Apenas el 2,2% (161 personas) presentaba irregularidades menores, tales como simples faltas administrativas.

Mientras que 4,1% de los hostigados eran ciudadanos argentinos. Tal como denuncia el CELS: «los datos dan cuenta de que este tipo de operativos solo tienen intención de

 montar un gran espectáculo sobre la intervención policial».


Foto extraida de Página 12. Sin crédito de autor/a.


El 53% de las intervenciones se ejecutó en la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, apuntando específicamente a las comunas 9, 3 y 7 (Liniers, Balvanera y Flores), zonas atravesadas por ferias populares y trabajadores de la economía informal. Del otro lado de la General Paz, el 72% de los operativos bonaerenses se concentró en el municipio de Lomas de Zamora. Ante la falta de un diagnóstico real, el Gobierno decide tratar a poblaciones que sostienen empleos de subsistencia, lisa y llanamente como un chivo expiatorio de la crisis económica.


En mayo de 2025, el Poder Ejecutivo impuso por decreto una reforma (Decreto 366/25) desde una mirada excluyente y criminalizadora, que echó por tierra el paradigma de integración sostenido durante los últimos 20 años.


El decreto exige acreditar «medios económicos suficientes» para acceder a la residencia. Pero un año después de su implementación, la propia Dirección Nacional de Migraciones reconoció que los criterios para evaluar esa solvencia aún están «a estudio de las autoridades superiores»

. Es decir, se exigen requisitos que no estan claros hoy.


Foto extraida de Izquierda diario. Sin crédito de autor/a.


El CELS es claro y advierte: «El gobierno produce el problema: al ralentizar los trámites migratorios, genera que más personas estén en condiciones de irregularidad y luego las persigue».


Desde la vigencia del mencionado decreto, el promedio de expulsiones dictadas se duplicó, pasando de 98 mensuales en 2025, a 202 en el primer semestre de 2026, con un alarmante pico de 379 casos solo en junio.


Las cifras confirman que no existe en Argentina un problema migratorio, sino

una decisión de una política enfocada en promover el racismo y la xenofobia institucional.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Jubilados/as de la Quinta de Olivos: otro territorio, la misma lucha
content:
Desde mayo de 2025, las y los jubilados de Vicente López empezaron a organizar protestas en la misma sintonía que ocurren en el Congreso. Se juntan los miércoles por la tarde y tienen un pliego de demandas asociadas a sus condiciones de vida y al derecho a la protesta.


Denunciando el genocidio silencioso de los adultos mayores el pasado 20 de agosto. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


Dialogamos con Liliana Russo, jubilada de esa organización, quien nos comentó cómo vienen sosteniendo la lucha: “Nosotros nos reunimos todos los miércoles en la avenida Maipú, frente a la quinta presidencial, en la esquina de Villate, a las 5 de la tarde en invierno y a las 6 de la tarde en verano. Bueno, queremos contarles que nosotros venimos haciendo esto desde hace casi un año y medio. Empezamos en mayo del año pasado, éramos 4 personas, y, bueno, ahora estamos de una manera sostenida, todos los miércoles con frío, calor, lluvia, lo que suceda, y somos más o menos 30, 40 personas de manera permanente”.
